common_name: Star Bright Dumb Cane (Narrow-Leaf Variegated Dieffenbachia)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained, fertile potting mix; Star Bright is frost-tender and grown outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere as an indoor foliage plant.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained, fertile potting mix. Star Bright is a University of Florida breeding-program release distinguished by unusually long, narrow leaves in a three-tone pattern of green, yellow-green, and cream that give the plant a finer, more feathery texture than broader-leaved dumb cane cultivars. Its slender leaf form and dense, upright habit make it a striking accent among bolder tropical foliage without dominating a shaded grouping. Water when the top inch of potting mix dries, avoid cold drafts and temperatures below 60°F, and wear gloves when handling or pruning, since the sap contains calcium oxalate crystals that severely irritate skin and the mouth if chewed.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Mid-Florida Research and Education Center — 'Star Bright' Dieffenbachia breeding release

common_name: Tropic Honey Dumb Cane (Golden Compact Dieffenbachia)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained, fertile potting mix; Tropic Honey is frost-tender and grown outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere as an indoor foliage plant.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained, fertile, consistently moist potting mix. Tropic Honey is a compact University of Florida hybrid, bred from 'Victory' and 'Tropic Marianne', with broad leaves washed in bright yellow-green to golden tones and a dense, well-branched habit that fills out a container quickly without becoming leggy. Its compact growth and vivid coloring make it a favorite for smaller interior spaces where a full-sized dumb cane would outgrow the room. Note that Tropic Honey is notably sensitive to chilling injury, so keep it above 55°F and away from cold drafts or air conditioning vents; keep the sap, which contains irritating calcium oxalate crystals, away from children and pets.
sources: University of Florida IFAS — 'Tropic Honey' Dieffenbachia (HortScience)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained, fertile potting mix; Triumph is frost-tender and grown outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere as an indoor foliage plant.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained, fertile potting mix. Triumph was the first hybrid released from the University of Florida's dieffenbachia breeding program, combining the bold cream-and-green leaf variegation of 'Camille' with a bright white midrib, held on short, clasping petioles that give it a dense, compact silhouette compared to older open-habit cultivars. The petioles themselves are notably ornamental, banded in russet and pink around a white core that deepens in color as the plant matures. Water when the top inch of potting mix dries, avoid temperatures below 60°F, and wear gloves when pruning or repotting, since the sap's calcium oxalate crystals cause painful irritation of skin and mouth.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Mid-Florida Research and Education Center — 'Triumph' Dieffenbachia breeding release (HortScience)

planting.note: Grow in deep shade to bright indirect light as a large houseplant, conservatory specimen, or outdoor shade planting in frost-free zones; Dieffenbachia bowmannii is one of the largest species in the genus and needs generous floor space to reach full size.

directions: Grow in bright indirect light to fairly deep shade in rich, well-drained, humus-heavy soil or potting mix kept evenly moist; native to Colombia and northern Brazil, Dieffenbachia bowmannii is among the largest and most dramatic species in the genus, forming thick canes topped with huge, softly textured leaves that can exceed two feet long, marked with pale green to whitish feathering along the veins. It makes an outstanding architectural specimen for conservatories, atriums, or shaded tropical landscapes in zones 10-12, where its scale rivals that of a small tree fern or philodendron. Give it room to spread, protect it from any chill below 55°F, and handle cut canes and foliage with gloves, since all parts contain calcium oxalate crystals that severely irritate skin, mouth, and throat if chewed.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens Kew — Plants of the World Online, Dieffenbachia bowmannii
Missouri Botanical Garden — Revision of Dieffenbachia (Araceae) for Central America, Annals of the Missouri Botanical Garden

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained, humus-rich potting mix; Dieffenbachia oerstedii is a smaller, clustering species that stays under three feet, well suited to tabletop or floor groupings.

directions: Grow in shade to bright indirect light in consistently moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil or potting mix; native from central Mexico through Central America to Ecuador, Dieffenbachia oerstedii is unusual within the genus for its mostly solid deep-green leaves, marked only by a single creamy-white stripe down the midrib rather than the speckled or blotched variegation typical of most dumb canes. It grows as a shorter, freely clustering subshrub with C-shaped, whitish-based petioles, making it a good understory or foreground choice among taller, bolder-patterned dieffenbachias. Keep it out of direct sun and below 55°F, and wear gloves when cutting or dividing clumps, since the sap's calcium oxalate crystals cause intense burning and temporary loss of speech if chewed, hence the common name dumb cane.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens Kew — Plants of the World Online, Dieffenbachia oerstedii
United States National Plant Germplasm System — Dieffenbachia oerstedii taxon profile
